label: My disruptive internal state is ADHD-driven rather than anxiety-, sleep-, or mood-driven
summary: The load-bearing personal hypothesis. Three rival mechanisms confound it and none has been ruled out; it cannot advance until the internal state is described concretely.

label: My ASRS result places me on the ADHD trait continuum rather than in a yes/no category
summary: Framing rather than diagnosis: a Part A score at the cutoff situates me somewhere on a spectrum the literature treats dimensionally.

label: ADHD's latent structure is dimensional (a continuum), not a discrete taxon
summary: Taxometric analyses of ADHD symptom data repeatedly fail to recover a category boundary and instead fit a continuous latent dimension. Contested: some analyses recover categorical structure within clinical samples.

label: Clinical ADHD is the quantitative extreme of a continuously distributed, heritable trait
summary: Twin and molecular-genetic evidence that the same aetiological factors operate across the whole symptom range, so the diagnosis marks a position on a continuum rather than a distinct condition.

label: The DSM symptom-count threshold is an arbitrary cut on a continuum with no natural breakpoint
summary: Impairment and quality of life decline linearly across the trait range with no discontinuity, so any diagnostic cutoff is a clinical convention. Held live by the counter-argument that unbounded threshold-lowering risks overdiagnosis and net harm.

label: Major dimensional frameworks (RDoC, HiTOP, the p-factor) place ADHD within continuous, transdiagnostic spectra
summary: The leading post-DSM classification programmes are all dimensional and locate ADHD on graded spectra (externalizing/disinhibition, general psychopathology) rather than in a discrete box.

label: A positive ASRS screen warrants a full clinical evaluation
summary: The actionable claim. Holds regardless of how the ADHD-vs-mimics question resolves — the evaluation is what resolves it.

label: Higher ADHD-like traits are associated with weaker response inhibition
summary: Research-side claim, replicated by the Horváth study in a non-clinical sample and under dual-task load.

label: Rising ADHD-trait load progressively flattens the inhibition–learning trade-off
summary: The paper's core result: the compensatory learning advantage that normally accompanies weak inhibition breaks down at the high end of the trait continuum.

label: Inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are distinct but strongly correlated, not orthogonal
summary: At the phenotype level the two DSM domains share a dominant general factor (latent r ≈ .68–.78); a bifactor structure fits best, so the domains are oblique rather than independent axes.

label: Rating-based and task-based measures of the same construct are only weakly related
summary: Questionnaire and performance measures of executive function correlate at about median r = .19 and assess different levels of cognition — so the two instrument families are near-orthogonal, not interchangeable.

label: ADHD arises through dissociable neurocognitive pathways, present in some individuals but not others
summary: Inhibitory, delay/reward and timing deficits are independent components whose co-occurrence is no greater than chance, and no single deficit is universal — the mechanism level is genuinely near-orthogonal.

label: No single instrument is diagnostic; valid assessment is multi-method across levels
summary: Ratings and tasks disagree, the best objective tasks are not decisive, and robust markers like reaction-time variability are not ADHD-specific — so discriminating ADHD (and its mimics) requires a multi-method evaluation, not one measure.

label: ADHD measures separate ADHD from healthy controls, but not from the mimics
summary: Ratings and tasks alike discriminate ADHD from typically developing controls, yet lose their edge against other clinical conditions — anxiety, mood, OCD — so no single instrument can rule out the differential. The measurement-side root of the ADHD-vs-anxiety tension.

label: Most adult-identified ADHD is late-identified rather than genuinely late-onset
summary: Birth cohorts found adult and childhood ADHD groups barely overlap, but careful repeated assessment excludes ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases; survivors show childhood symptoms masked by cognitive strength. Compensation plus rising demand, not new onset.

label: The course of ADHD fluctuates rather than simply persisting or remitting
summary: Most of the MTA sample showed waxing and waning persistence and remission rather than stable persistence or recovery, making person-environment fit the appropriate frame — the temporal counterpart of the dimensional argument.

label: The ADHD sex ratio largely reflects referral and ascertainment, not underlying prevalence
summary: Clinic ratios far exceed community ratios in the same populations, high-symptom girls are diagnosed less often than high-symptom boys, and the gap narrows to ~1.5:1 in adulthood — the signature of under-detection rather than a true prevalence difference.

label: The arousal/state-regulation axis is shared with the mimics by construction, not by coincidence
summary: The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep-wake cycle and noise — so sleep debt and anxiety move the very variable ADHD is hypothesised to dysregulate. What may be ADHD-specific is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

label: Excessive mind-wandering is transdiagnostic rather than an ADHD marker
summary: Mind-wandering tracked anxiety independently of ADHD diagnosis and showed no categorical ADHD/non-ADHD difference, while correlating with inattention dimensionally — and it mediates ADHD symptoms' relationship to anxiety and depression.

label: Sleep debt is a strong rival for inattention but a weak one for internal restlessness
summary: Experimental sleep restriction reliably degrades attention and emotional lability in healthy people, but no experiment has shown it induces hyperactivity or impulsivity — narrowing which half of the picture sleep can explain.

label: Onset, trajectory and counterfactual — not symptom intensity — discriminate ADHD from anxiety
summary: Because both conditions produce internal restlessness and the rating items measuring it are partly anxiety items, the discriminating evidence is structural: whether the restlessness predates any anxiety, persists in its absence, is situational or constant, and whether its content is worry or topic-shifting.

label: The 'calm outside, churning inside' state is internalized hyperactivity — subjective restlessness — not overt motor hyperactivity
summary: DSM allows adult hyperactivity to present as subjective restlessness, and adults with ADHD report mental restlessness in place of fidgeting; the IRS measures it and separates ADHD from non-ADHD students. This reframes the internal state as the adult form of the hyperactive axis — but the same internalized presentation is where anxiety is hardest to distinguish from ADHD.

label: Cognitive disengagement (daydreamy, foggy, mentally slow) is a construct distinct from ADHD inattention and more tied to internalizing
summary: Factor-analytic and meta-analytic work separates cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly SCT) from ADHD inattention and links it more to depression/internalizing than to hyperactivity/impulsivity. If the internal state is foggy and disengaged rather than restless, CDS — not ADHD hyperactivity — may be the better description, and it points toward the mood differential.

label: ADHD and anxiety co-occur far above chance across the lifespan
summary: Adult ADHD is highly comorbid with other DSM disorders, up to ~80% carry at least one, and ~25% of children with ADHD have an anxiety disorder. High comorbidity is why the ADHD-vs-anxiety differential is genuinely hard rather than a technicality — the two really do travel together.

label: Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, not merely a comorbidity
summary: Emotion dysregulation is prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major contributor to impairment, and has been called a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD. But its status is explicitly unsettled: it is equally consistent with being a correlated-but-distinct dimension or a separate entity, so 'core' is one reading among three.

label: The DSM childhood-onset requirement is hard to verify from an adult's own recall, so collateral information matters
summary: DSM needs some symptoms present in childhood, but adult self-recall of childhood ADHD has a positive predictive value near 0.27, and young adults with ADHD tend to underreport. Guidelines therefore lean on contemporaneous records and collateral informants (a parent or partner). This bears directly on a first evaluation in adulthood with no childhood documentation.
